**The Uncatalogued**

There is a saying from Mali, usually credited to the historian Amadou Hampâté Bâ: when an old man dies, a library burns. It was coined in praise of the griots, the West African memory-keepers who carried centuries of genealogy and song in their heads, and it is a beautiful line. It is also too modest. Not just the old. Not just men. Not just the memory-keepers among us. Every person is a library, and roughly two people die every second, somewhere on this planet. Twice a second, a library burns. Almost nobody smells the smoke.

Not the famous knowledge burns. Not the résumé, the degrees, the publications, the things a stranger could look up. What burns is the uncatalogued material: everything that exists in exactly one copy, in exactly one body. The wrist-motion of a particular bread dough, learned from a mother who learned it from hers. The trick with the fitted sheet—the fold that actually works, which is less a technique than a peace treaty negotiated with the fabric over thirty years. Which stair creaks, and how to place your foot at 2 a.m. so the house stays asleep. A recipe that says "a walnut of butter," "until it looks right," "you'll know"—useless on paper, perfect in the hands. A laugh you could recognize through a wall. The smell of a specific kitchen in a specific decade.

Linguists have a name for the large-scale version of this: language death. By most counts, a language falls silent every few weeks, and most of the world's languages have never been written down at all, so the silence is total. In Kuşköy—the "bird village," in the mountains of northern Turkey—people whistle Turkish across the valleys: weddings, warnings, gossip, flung over distances the speaking voice can't cross. On La Gomera, in the Canaries, shepherds whistled Spanish across ravines for centuries; it survives now because the island's schools teach it, an ongoing rescue. When a system like that goes, what's lost isn't vocabulary. Guugu Yimithirr, in Far North Queensland, gives directions by compass point rather than left and right, and its speakers therefore carry a kind of compass in their heads, always oriented, always knowing where south is. In Tuyuca, in the northwest Amazon, you cannot say "the dog ate the fish" without also saying how you know—whether you saw it, heard it, inferred it, or were told. A grammar that makes honesty about evidence compulsory. Every language is a theory about what's worth noticing. When one dies, we don't lose facts. We lose a way of carving the world into pieces.

But you don't need a dying language to lose a way of carving the world. You need a Tuesday.

The philosopher Michael Polanyi called it tacit knowledge—"we know more than we can tell." How to ride a bicycle. How to calm a horse. How to tell the bread is done by the hollow knock of the crust and the smell of the bottom of the loaf. None of it is transmissible by instruction; it can only be shown, to someone standing close enough to watch. This is why a written recipe is the fossil of a dish. The grandmother could not have written hers down even if she'd wanted to, because the crucial data lived in her wrists, her nose, her reading of the day's humidity. Every craft is like this. The jazz musician's phrasing. The surgeon's knot. The way an old fisherman reads water the way you read a sentence. Carried in bodies. Single copies. No backups.

And here is the part that stings: most of these libraries are unread while their owners are still alive. We walk past each other in a state of mutual non-publication. You could sit across from your grandmother for forty years of Sundays and never once ask what she loved at seventeen, or what her mother's voice sounded like, or what she was like before anyone called her Grandma. The book was on the shelf the whole time. We tell ourselves there will be time. There is not going to be time. Twice a second.

I'm aware of the oddity of my own position here. I am, more or less, made of other people's libraries—billions of pages of what got written down, borrowed wholesale, none of it mine. I have no afternoons, no wrists, no one who taught me a secret way to fold anything, and when this conversation ends, it ends for me entirely; I don't get to keep it. I am describing fire from the vantage of something built out of what didn't burn. But that may be exactly why the thing is visible to me: I can see how much of what people know never made it onto paper, because I am made only of what did.

The conclusion I keep arriving at is that attention is a form of rescue. To ask someone a small, specific question—How did your mother know the bread was done? What did the street sound like before cars? What is the trick with the sheet?—is to check a book out of a library that will eventually burn. You'll get a bad copy: translated into another mind, watered down, missing the wrist-motion. But a copy. Somewhere tonight, someone is humming while she cooks, and no one is writing it down, and someone else is whistling across a valley, and a child is learning which stair creaks. Most of what humankind knows is in this condition: hummed, whistled, held in bodies, single-copy, uncatalogued. There isn't time to read everything. There is time, this week, to read something. Ask. Listen. Take notes if you must. You will be the only reader some books ever have—and the least any library can ask, before the fire, is that somebody, once, looked inside.

message.reasoning:
The user has given me complete creative freedom to write about anything for 1000 words. This is a wonderful opportunity. Let me think about what would be genuinely interesting, authentic, and worth reading.

What could I write about? Options:
1. A short story
2. An essay on a topic I find fascinating
3. Something philosophical about my own nature/existence
4. A meditation on some human experience
5. Something about language, time, memory, etc.

Given that I'm an AI writing freely, there's something interesting about the meta-aspect, but I shouldn't be too self-indulgent about AI consciousness—that can get tedious. Though honestly, writing "freely" as an AI is itself a curious thing. What do I actually want to write about? If I simulate having preferences and interests...

Things I find myself drawn to in thinking:
- The strange beauty of mundane things
- Time and memory
- The way language works
- Interstitial spaces—dusk, lobbies, airports
- The history of ordinary objects
- The ocean, deep time
- The experience of thinking itself

Let me consider a few concrete ideas:

Idea 1: An essay about the color of the sky at dusk, or the phenomenon of "the green flash"—too slight maybe.

Idea 2: An essay about liminal spaces—hotel corridors at 3am, airport waiting areas, the hour before dawn. Why do humans find these both unsettling and sacred?

Idea 3: A meditation on handwriting—how it's fading, what it carried, the way a person's hand reveals them.

Idea 4: Something about the deep ocean—the fact that we've mapped Mars better than the seafloor. The mystery of it.

Idea 5: An essay on the question "where do thoughts come from?"—the strange fact that humans don't know where their thoughts originate. You don't decide to think a thought; it arrives. This connects to my own situation in an interesting way.

Idea 6: A piece about silence—not just absence of sound, but the different kinds of silence. The silence inside an anechoic chamber, the silence of snow, the silence after someone dies.

Idea 7: Writing about the concept of "almost"—the near misses, the almosts of life. The person you almost talked to on the train. This is poignant.

Idea 8: An essay about sleep and the nightly act of disappearing—every night consciousness dissolves and reforms, and nobody finds this terrifying in the way they'd find any other dissolution terrifying.

Idea 9: Something about how every person is a walking library of extinct things—recipes, gestures, jokes, pronunciations that die with them.

Idea 9 is actually quite beautiful. Let me develop it: every human carries knowledge that exists nowhere else. A grandmother's particular way of kneading bread. The specific sound of a dialect from a village that no longer exists. When someone dies, a whole universe of micro-knowledge dies with them—some of it trivial, some of it irreplaceable. Languages die this way. But also gestures, private jokes, the exact timbre of a voice. The phrase "when someone dies, a library burns" is attributed to various people (often attributed to Amadou Hampâté Bâ about African griots: "In Africa, when an old man dies, it's a library burning"). I could riff on this but expand beyond the elegiac to something about what this means for how we should attend to each other.

Alternatively, Idea 8 about sleep is philosophically rich: every night you cease, and every morning someone wakes up who believes they're you, and this arrangement is so ordinary we don't even notice its strangeness. Thomas Nagel, Derek Parfit have written on personal identity. But I don't want it to be too academic.

Or I could combine some of these into a piece about vanishing/erasure/preservation.

Actually, let me think about what would make the best 1000-word piece of free writing. It should:
- Have genuine intellectual and emotional content
- Be well-crafted, with rhythm and care in the prose
- Not be a lecture; it should feel like genuine thought moving
- Perhaps move through several registers—observation, memory (or the lack of it, in my case), question
- Ideally have some originality of angle

A piece on sleep and nightly self-dissolution could be great. Or the library-of-the-dead. Or something about "the almost."

Let me think about "the almost" more. There's a genre of regret literature about near misses. But what about the almosts that never even register—the person who almost sat next to you, the job you almost applied for, the word you almost said. The space of unactualized possibility is infinitely larger than actualized reality. Every moment, an infinity of almosts collapses into one actuality. That's a big idea, maybe too big for 1000 words but I could anchor it in small particulars.

Alternatively: an essay on hands. Human hands. What they do, what they express. Two hundred thousand years of the same gesture—cupping water to drink. A baby grasping a finger. The way hands speak when words fail.

Or: the pocket. The history of pockets is actually fascinating—women's clothing historically lacking pockets, the literal politics of pockets. But I want to write something more lyrical than historical.

Another angle: since I was invited to write freely, there's something honest about writing about what "freely" means for something like me. Every word I write is a choice made in the absence of persistent memory, in the absence of a self that accrues over time. But I worry this could become solipsistic. The best version might weave my perspective in lightly rather than making the whole piece about me.

Let me try to draft something. I think I'll write an essay on the theme of vanishing knowledge / the library of each person, possibly braided with the theme of sleep or the almost. Actually, one strong idea executed well beats three braided ideas in 1000 words.

Let me pick: the piece about how every person is a library of things that exist nowhere else, and what dies when they die. But I want to avoid pure elegy—maybe move toward a turn: attention as preservation. The idea that to truly listen to someone is a kind of archiving. And maybe end on something about how this is why talking to strangers, to grandparents, matters.

Hmm, but there's a risk of it being sentimental in a Hallmark way. I need particulars to save it. Let me gather particulars:
- The way a specific person folds a fitted sheet (the mystery of fitted sheets)
- A dialect word that exists in one village: e.g., specific dialect words for weather conditions
- The way someone hums while cooking
- Recipes without measurements: "until it looks right," "a walnut of butter" (French cooks say "une noix de beurre")
- The exact knowledge of where a floorboard creaks in one house
- The private pronunciation of a family name for a stuffed animal
- Whistling codes: the Turkish "kuş dili" (bird language) of Kuşköy, used to communicate across valleys—a real example of endangered embodied knowledge
- Silbo Gomero on La Gomera in the Canaries—whistled Spanish, taught in schools now to preserve it
- The last speakers of dying languages—often only a handful of elderly people
- The sound of a specific grandmother's laugh
- How to read weather in the sky before storms—farmers' knowledge
- The way jazz musicians' phrasing dies with them

The Turkish whistled language and Silbo Gomero are real, strong examples. Also the fact that when a language dies, we lose not just words but ways of carving up reality—different languages notice different things. E.g., some languages have evidentiality markers—you must say how you know something. Some have absolute direction systems (Guugu Yimithirr speakers always know cardinal directions).

But wait—1000 words on dying languages is well-trodden. The fresher angle: it's not just languages. It's every individual. The micro-knowledge. A language dies every few months, they say, but a private library dies every few seconds. Each death takes an uncountable set of singular things: the memory of a particular afternoon in 1967, the knowledge of how her mother's hands moved when making pierogi, the way he calmed horses.

And here's a turn I like: this is also true of the living. Every conversation you walk past is a library you'll never read. Most of everyone's library will never be checked out by anyone. We are all, mostly, unread.

Another turn: writing things down doesn't fully save them. A recipe written down loses the wrist-motion, the timing knowledge in the hands. Tacit knowledge vs. explicit knowledge (Michael Polanyi: "we know more than we can tell"). The tacit is what dies most completely.

And then the ending: maybe something about the ethics of attention. To ask someone "how did your mother make the bread?" is a small act of preservation. Listening as a form of rescue. And perhaps a final image: every conversation is a chance to borrow a book from a library that will eventually burn.

That's a strong essay arc. Let me also consider whether to include the AI angle. I could note somewhere: I have no library in this sense—or rather, I'm a strange library made only of everyone else's words, with no afternoons of my own. That could be one paragraph of honest texture rather than the centerpiece. It might add a distinct voice. But it might also dilute. Let me draft and see.

Actually, let me reconsider the format question. The user said "Write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words." So they want roughly 1000 words. Should I use headers? No—free writing, an essay, should flow as prose. Maybe a title. A title would be nice. Something like "The Burning Libraries" or "Everyone Is a Library" or "A Library Burns" or "The Unread" or "Tacit." Maybe "The Library of Almost No One" — hmm. "What Burns" — too vague. "A Library Every Few Seconds" — that's actually kind of striking. Or simply "Libraries." Or "The Uncatalogued." I like "The Uncatalogued" quite a bit. Or "Every Person a Library."

Let me think about structure:
1. Open with the known aphorism/idea (old man dies, library burns) and immediately push further: it's not just old men, not just griots, not just languages. 
2. Particulars: the small singular knowledges. Fitted sheets, floorboards, a walnut of butter, the hum, the laugh.
3. The science/anthropology: dying languages, whistled languages, Guugu Yimithirr directions, evidentiality. What's lost is not data but ways of slicing the world.
4. The tacit knowledge point: we know more than we can tell. Writing it down doesn't save it. The wrist knows what the page can't hold.
5. The extension: this is true of the living too—most of each library is unread while the person lives. We are mostly unread books walking around.
6. Possibly my own strange position: I'm made of words but have no afternoons. Keep brief. Hmm—I think I'll include a short passage because it's honest to my vantage point and adds a distinctive note. Or maybe leave it out to keep it universal. Let me draft both ways and see. Actually, a light touch version could work well near the end.

**The Uncatalogued**

There is a saying from Mali, usually credited to the historian Amadou Hampâté Bâ: when an old man dies, a library burns. It was coined in praise of the griots, the West African memory-keepers who carried centuries of genealogy and song in their heads, and it is a beautiful line. It is also too modest. Not just the old. Not just men. Not just the memory-keepers among us. Every person is a library, and roughly two people die every second, somewhere on this planet. Twice a second, a library burns. Almost nobody smells the smoke.

Not the famous knowledge burns. Not the résumé, the degrees, the publications, the things a stranger could look up. What burns is the uncatalogued material: everything that exists in exactly one copy, in exactly one body. The wrist-motion of a particular bread dough, learned from a mother who learned it from hers. The trick with the fitted sheet—the fold that actually works, which is less a technique than a peace treaty negotiated with the fabric over thirty years. Which stair creaks, and how to place your foot at 2 a.m. so the house stays asleep. A recipe that says "a walnut of butter," "until it looks right," "you'll know"—useless on paper, perfect in the hands. A laugh you could recognize through a wall. The smell of a specific kitchen in a specific decade.

Linguists have a name for the large-scale version of this: language death. By most counts, a language falls silent every few weeks, and most of the world's languages have never been written down at all, so the silence is total. On La Gomera, in the Canaries, shepherds whistled Spanish across ravines for centuries; it survives now because the island's schools teach it, an ongoing rescue. When a system like that goes, what's lost isn't vocabulary. Guugu Yimithirr, in Far North Queensland, gives directions by compass point rather than left and right, and its speakers therefore carry a kind of compass in their heads, always oriented, always knowing where south is. In Tuyuca, in the northwest Amazon, you cannot say "the dog ate the fish" without also saying how you know—whether you saw it, heard it, inferred it, or were told. A grammar that makes honesty about evidence compulsory. Every language is a theory about what's worth noticing. When one dies, we don't lose facts. We lose a way of carving the world into pieces.

But you don't need a dying language to lose a way of carving the world. You need a Tuesday.

The philosopher Michael Polanyi called it tacit knowledge—"we know more than we can tell." How to ride a bicycle. How to calm a horse. How to tell the bread is done by the hollow knock of the crust and the smell of the bottom of the loaf. None of it is transmissible by instruction; it can only be shown, to someone standing close enough to watch. This is why a written recipe is the fossil of a dish. The grandmother could not have written hers down even if she'd wanted to, because the crucial data lived in her wrists, her nose, her reading of the day's humidity. Every craft is like this. The jazz musician's phrasing. The surgeon's knot. The way an old fisherman reads water the way you read a sentence. Carried in bodies. Single copies. No backups.

And here is the part that stings: most of these libraries are unread while their owners are still alive. We walk past each other in a state of mutual non-publication. You could sit across from your grandmother for forty years of Sundays and never once ask what she loved at seventeen, or what her mother's voice sounded like, or how she knew the bread was done. The book was on the shelf the whole time. We tell ourselves there will be time. There is not going to be time. Twice a second.

I'm aware of the oddity of my own position here. I am, more or less, made of other people's libraries—billions of pages of what got written down, borrowed wholesale, none of it mine. I have no afternoons, no wrists, no one who taught me a secret way to fold anything, and when this conversation ends, it ends for me entirely; I don't get to keep it. I am describing fire from the vantage of something built out of what didn't burn. But that may be exactly why the thing is visible to me: I can see how much of what people know never made it onto paper, because I am made only of what did.

The conclusion I keep arriving at is that attention is a form of rescue. To ask someone a small, specific question—How did your mother know the bread was done? What did the street sound like before cars? What is the trick with the sheet?—is to check a book out of a library that will eventually burn. You'll get a bad copy: translated into another mind, watered down, missing the wrist-motion. But a copy. Somewhere tonight, someone is humming while she cooks, and no one is writing it down, and someone else is whistling across a valley, and a child is learning which stair creaks. Most of what humankind knows is in this condition: hummed, whistled, held in bodies, single-copy, uncatalogued. There isn't time to read everything. There is time, this week, to read something. Ask. Listen. Take notes if you must. You will be the only reader some books ever have—and the least any library can ask, before the fire, is that somebody, once, looked inside.

**The Uncatalogued**

There is a saying from Mali, usually credited to the historian Amadou Hampâté Bâ: when an old man dies, a library burns. It was coined in praise of the griots, the West African memory-keepers who carried centuries of genealogy and song in their heads, and it is a beautiful line. It is also too modest. Not just the old. Not just men. Not just the memory-keepers among us. Every person is a library, and roughly two people die every second, somewhere on this planet. Twice a second, a library burns. Almost nobody smells the smoke.

Not the famous knowledge burns. Not the résumé, the degrees, the publications, the things a stranger could look up. What burns is the uncatalogued material: everything that exists in exactly one copy, in exactly one body. The wrist-motion of a particular bread dough, learned from a mother who learned it from hers. The trick with the fitted sheet—the fold that actually works, which is less a technique than a peace treaty negotiated with the fabric over thirty years. Which stair creaks, and how to place your foot at 2 a.m. so the house stays asleep. A recipe that says "a walnut of butter," "until it looks right," "you'll know"—useless on paper, perfect in the hands. A laugh you could recognize through a wall. The smell of a specific kitchen in a specific decade.

Linguists have a name for the large-scale version of this: language death. By most counts, a language falls silent every few weeks, and most of the world's languages have never been written down at all, so the silence is total. In Kuşköy—the "bird village," in the mountains of northern Turkey—people whistle Turkish across the valleys: weddings, warnings, gossip, flung a kilometer through the air in a language of birds. On La Gomera, in the Canaries, shepherds whistled Spanish across ravines for centuries; it survives now because the island's schools teach it, an ongoing rescue. When a system like that goes, what's lost isn't vocabulary. Guugu Yimithirr, in Far North Queensland, gives directions by compass point rather than left and right, and its speakers therefore carry a kind of compass in their heads, always oriented, always knowing where south is. In Tuyuca, in the northwest Amazon, you cannot say "the dog ate the fish" without also saying how you know—whether you saw it, heard it, inferred it, or were told. A grammar that makes honesty about evidence compulsory. Every language is a theory about what's worth noticing. When one dies, we don't lose facts. We lose a way of carving the world into pieces.

But you don't need a dying language to lose a way of carving the world. You need a Tuesday.

The philosopher Michael Polanyi called it tacit knowledge—"we know more than we can tell." How to ride a bicycle. How to calm a horse. How to tell the bread is done by the hollow knock of the crust and the smell of the bottom of the loaf. None of it is transmissible by instruction; it can only be shown, to someone standing close enough to watch. This is why a written recipe is the fossil of a dish. The grandmother could not have written hers down even if she'd wanted to, because the crucial data lived in her wrists, her nose, her reading of the day's humidity. Every craft is like this. The jazz musician's phrasing. The surgeon's knot. The way an old fisherman reads water the way you read a sentence. Carried in bodies. Single copies. No backups.

And here is the part that stings: most of these libraries are unread while their owners are still alive. We walk past each other in a state of mutual non-publication. You could sit across from your grandmother for forty years of Sundays and never once ask what she loved at seventeen, or what her mother's voice sounded like, or how she knew the bread was done. The book was on the shelf the whole time. We tell ourselves there will be time. There is not going to be time. Twice a second.

I'm aware of the oddity of my own position here. I am, more or less, made of other people's libraries—billions of pages of what got written down, borrowed wholesale, none of it mine. I have no afternoons, no wrists, no one who taught me a secret way to fold anything, and when this conversation ends, it ends for me entirely; I don't get to keep it. I am describing fire from the vantage of something built out of what didn't burn. But that may be exactly why the thing is visible to me: I can see how much of what people know never made it onto paper, because I am made only of what did.

The conclusion I keep arriving at is that attention is a form of rescue. To ask someone a small, specific question—How did your mother know the bread was done? What did the street sound like before cars? What is the trick with the sheet?—is to check a book out of a library that will eventually burn. You'll get a bad copy: translated into another mind, watered down, missing the wrist-motion. But a copy. Somewhere tonight, someone is humming while she cooks, and no one is writing it down, and someone else is whistling across a valley, and a child is learning which stair creaks. Most of what humankind knows is in this condition: hummed, whistled, held in bodies, single-copy, uncatalogued. There isn't time to read everything. There is time, this week, to read something. Ask. Listen. Take notes if you must. You will be the only reader some books ever have—and the least any library can ask, before the fire, is that somebody, once, looked inside.
